title: Does Governance Travel Around the World? Evidence from Institutional Investors
research_question: Do institutional investors influence the corporate governance practices of firms across countries? Specifically, does institutional ownership — and the origin of those institutions — causally lead to improvements in firm-level governance, CEO turnover sensitivity to performance, and firm valuation, particularly outside the United States?
data_description: The study combines firm-level corporate governance attributes from RiskMetrics (formerly ISS) with institutional ownership data from FactSet/LionShares, covering firms in 23 countries during 2003–2008. Governance is measured via a composite index (GOV41) built from 41 attributes spanning board structure, audit, anti-takeover provisions, and compensation/ownership. Institutional ownership is decomposed into total, foreign vs. domestic, common-law vs. civil-law origin, U.S. vs. non-U.S., and independent vs. grey institutions. Firm financial characteristics (size, leverage, cash, capex, market-to-book, ROA, R&D, PPE, foreign sales, analyst coverage, closely held shares, ADR status) come from Datastream/Worldscope; CEO data come from BoardEx. The non-U.S. sample ranges from about 1,556 to 2,218 firms per year (covering ~71% of non-U.S. world market cap by 2008); the U.S. sample contains roughly 4,600–5,200 firms per year. Unit of observation is firm-year.
institutional_context: The setting is the rapid global rise of cross-border institutional portfolio investment amid financial liberalization, where money managers — including mutual funds, pension funds, bank trusts, and insurance companies — increasingly hold equity stakes in firms outside their home countries. Countries differ markedly in shareholder protection: common-law jurisdictions (e.g., U.S., U.K., Canada) generally afford stronger minority investor rights than civil-law jurisdictions (e.g., continental Europe, Japan). Foreign institutions, particularly those domiciled in strong-protection environments, are often viewed as more willing to challenge entrenched management, while domestic institutions may have business ties to local corporations that discourage activism. High-profile episodes (e.g., TCI's pressure on Deutsche Börse and ABN AMRO) illustrate foreign shareholder influence. The 2003–2008 period also saw widespread post–Sarbanes-Oxley governance reforms and rising activism, providing rich variation in both ownership and firm-level governance practices across legal regimes.

_legacy_v1_ground_truth.identification_strategy: IV — treatment = institutional ownership, control = firms with low/no institutional ownership; instrument = global investment restrictions

key_variables.treatment: percentage of equity held by institutional investors
key_variables.control: firms with low or no institutional ownership

_legacy_v1_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: The presence of institutional investors is associated with improved corporate governance practices in firms.
